abstract: Canonical models of the macroscopic human connectome are dominated through static, cortico-centric networks by positive functional correlates. Yet naturalistic behavior demands fluid topological reconfigurations, wherein biologically critical functional antagonism (negative correlates) is routinely discarded as noise. Meanwhile, deep subcortical control remains overlooked. Here, we develop the Spatial Connectivity Cycle Flexibility (SCCF) framework to track whole-brain community dynamics across signed interactions. We show that canonical static networks reflect time-averaged projections of an underlying dynamic probability landscape, actively orchestrated by three (basal, regulatory, and fast) conserved subcortical routing modes. Individual dynamic modular co-occurrence function-prints predict 16 independent behavioral dimensions across cognitive, personality, and physiological domains, indicating that behavioral heterogeneity depends on the dynamic balance between network integration and antagonistic segregation. Crucially, independent cross-cohort validation reveals an organizational duality: subcortical routing for core cognitive computation is broadly conserved across cultures, whereas socio-emotional circuits exhibit marked divergence aligned with distinct behavioral ecologies. These findings challenge prevailing cortico-centric and positive-only assumptions of the functional connectome, providing an exploratory computational framework that links subcortical routing and active network antagonism to human phenotypic diversity and behavioral adaptation.
